bibl.title: Political Discourse on Social Media: Echo Chambers, Gatekeepers, and the Price of Bipartisanship

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: When applied to discussions about politically contentious topics, our results support the existence of political echo chambers.

span.label: political echo chambers on social media
span.quote: This paper studies the phenomenon of political echo chambers on social media.

span.label: observational-data-analysis
span.quote: We use a collection of ten different datasets from Twitter, each of which contains a set of tweets on a given topic of discussion.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: content and network are measured JOINTLY at the level of the individual user, rather than content consumption alone, and the authors state that as the study's distinguishing move
span.quote: Unlike many previous works that focus on measuring only content consumption to quantify the echo-chamber effects, we study content consumption and production jointly at the level of individual users, and examine how different content profiles correlate with the network position of users. Though we are not the first to study echo chambers on Twitter, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to jointly use content and network to characterize echo chambers.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: POLITICAL LEANING IS NOT INFERRED FROM THE TEXT AT ALL: scoring short snippets is called very challenging, so the leaning is inherited from an externally supplied per-domain ground truth of news organisations
span.note: about this quote: Q-630, 2026-08-16: THIS QUOTE IS TRUNCATED MID-SENTENCE BECAUSE THE FILE INTERRUPTS IT. The staged text continues "...news organizations with 6https://en.wikipedia.org/... 7http://www.bbc.com/... 8https://www.nytimes.com/..." - three footnote URLs are spliced between 'with' and the rest of the clause, which resumes as 'a presence on social media obtained from Bakshy et al.' The span stops at the last word before the splice. The sentence is not quotable in full from this file without quoting three URLs in the middle of it.
span.quote: Obtaining a characterization of political leaning for short text snippets, such as tweets, is a very challenging problem, in general. To confront this challenge, we use a ground truth of political leaning scores of various news organizations with

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: and that borrowed score has a stated meaning of its own - the FRACTION OF FACEBOOK USERS VISITING A DOMAIN WHO IDENTIFY THEMSELVES AS CONSERVATIVE ON THEIR PROFILE - which the authors read as the domain having a conservative or liberal bent in its coverage
span.quote: The score takes values between 0 and 1 and expresses the fraction of Facebook users who visit these pages that identify themselves as conservative on their Facebook profile. A value close to 1 (0) indicates that the domain has a conservative (liberal) bent in their coverage.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the measurement is deliberately restricted to what can be scored: only tweets carrying a link to a news organisation with a known and independently derived leaning are counted at all
span.quote: To quantify the political leaning of content posted on Twitter, we consider only messages that contain a link to an online news organization with a known and independently derived political leaning. In particular, we use the dataset of the political leaning scores of news organizations described in Section 3.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: CONSUMPTION IS DEFINED THROUGH THE NETWORK: a user's produced content is the tweets they post, and their consumed content is the tweets posted by the accounts they follow
span.quote: For the content production of a user u, we consider tweets posted by user u. For the content consumption of a user u we consider tweets posted by users whom u follows.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: partisanship is given a PARAMETERISED definition rather than a threshold - a user is delta-partisan when their production polarity lies within delta of either extreme - and the authors state the nesting property that follows, so a claim at one delta implies the claim at every larger one
span.quote: We say that a user is δ -partisan, for some value 0 ≤ δ ≤ 1 2 , if their production polarity is within δ from either extreme value min{p(u), 1 − p(u)} ≤ δ . (2) The smaller the value of δ the more partisan a user is. Note also that if a user u is δ -partisan then u is also δ ′-partisan for δ < δ ′ ≤ 1

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: VARIANCE IS MEASURED ALONGSIDE THE MEAN over the same set of tweets, with the stated objective of quantifying the RANGE of opinions a user's produced content covers
span.quote: Besides the average political leaning of produced tweets, we also measure the variance in political leaning over the same set of tweets. The objective is to quantify the range of opinions of a user covered by the produced content.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: FIVE NON-POLITICAL DATASETS ARE COLLECTED AS A BASELINE for the political ones - tbt, ff, gameofthrones, love, foodporn - each built from one hashtag by parsing an archive, filtering to users with at least five tweets, and then taking all of those users' tweets
span.quote: To have a baseline for our measurements over the Political datasets, we also use five datasets that correspond to non-political topics, in particular: tbt (“throwback Thursday”), ff (“follow Friday”), gameofthrones, love, and foodporn. Each of these topics is associated with a particular hashtag (e.g., #tbt for tbt). The datasets are built as follows. First, we parse the tweets in the Internet Archive collection and select tweets that contain the corresponding hashtag for each topic during the month of June 2016. Second, we filter out users who have less than 5 tweets. Third, we obtain all tweets generated by these users.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: automated accounts are excluded by minimum AND maximum thresholds on tweets per day, followers and friends, together with a requirement that the account be at least one year old at collection time
span.quote: For all the datasets, we perform simple checks to remove bots, using minimum and maximum thresholds for number of tweets per day, followers, friends, and ensure that the account is at least one year old at the time of data collection.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the paper STIPULATES 'gatekeeper' against the established sense and says so: in communication studies the term names news media sources acting as filters, and here it names an individual user who receives content from both leanings but produces only one
span.quote: Gatekeeping is a term commonly used in communication studies to refer to news media sources that act as filters of information [27]. Barzilai-Nahon [8] propose a model based on network theory for gatekeeping which generalizes the concept of gatekeeping for the Internet and applies to all information types (not just news). Several studies have looked at gatekeeping practices on Twitter [25, 39] and conclude that unlike in traditional media, any common user can become a gatekeeper on social media. The definition of these gatekeepers on social media also differs from the traditional gatekeepers in media organizations, due to the alternative information pathways available to social media users. In our case, we define gatekeepers as users who receive content from both political leanings, but only produce content from a single leaning, thus “filtering” information from one side.

span.label: political leaning is measured only from tweets that link to news sources of known, independently-derived leaning, not the message content itself
span.note: what this limits: every political-leaning measurement in the study: WE CONSIDER ONLY MESSAGES THAT CONTAIN A LINK TO AN ONLINE NEWS ORGANIZATION WITH A KNOWN AND INDEPENDENTLY DERIVED POLITICAL [leaning] - users without such links are unmeasured
span.quote: To quantify the political leaning of content posted on Twitter, we consider only messages that contain a link to an online news organization with a known and independently derived political leaning.

span.label: All data come from Twitter and are only a sample of social-media discussion.
span.note: what this limits: the generalisation to political discourse at large: all data come from Twitter and are only a sample of social-media discussion
span.quote: First, the datasets used are just a sample of all the discussions in social media, and they all come from Twitter.

span.label: Results are drawn from politically-savvy users and should not be assumed to generalise to the general public.
span.note: what this limits: the network measured: the analysis rests on the retweet and follow graph available through the API, not on the full communication structure
span.quote: However, as we focused on politically-savvy users on Twitter, the reader should not infer that our observations generalize immediately to other settings, or that echo chamber effects are as pronounced for the general public.

span.label: The polarity measures depend on externally supplied political labels for news sources.
span.note: what this limits: every polarity score: OUR PRODUCTION AND CONSUMPTION SCORES RELY ON EXTERNAL LABELING OF NEWS SOURCES ALONG A POLITICAL AXIS
span.quote: Second, our production and consumption scores rely on external labeling of news sources along a political axis.

span.label: Following is used as a proxy for actual consumption; users may not read everything their neighbours post.
span.note: what this limits: every consumption measure: OUR ANALYSIS ASSUMES THAT EACH USER CONSUMES ALL CONTENT PRODUCED BY ALL THEIR NEIGHBORS - following stands in for reading
span.quote: Moreover, our analysis assumes that each user consumes all content produced by all their neighbors.

span.label: Some articles from the scored news domains may not be political.
span.note: what this limits: the political-content assumption: NOT ALL NEWS ARTICLES FROM THE NEWS SOURCES WE BASE THE POLARITY MEASURES [on] ARE POLITICAL
span.quote: Finally, it is possible that not all news articles from the news sources we base the polarity measures are political.

span.label: The causal relations between selective exposure, biased assimilation, algorithmic filtering and echo chambers are not addressed.
span.note: what this limits: any causal reading of echo chambers: UNDERSTANDING HOW ALL THESE PHENOMENA INTERACT WITH EACH OTHER AND THE PRECISE CAUSALITY RELATIONS IS BEYOND THE SCOPE OF THIS PAPER
span.quote: Understanding how all these phenomena interact with each other and the precise causality relations is beyond the scope of this paper.

span.label: The literature has no consensus definition of the paper's central term, so the authors chose one.
span.note: what this limits: the finding that echo chambers are prevalent: the authors state there is no consensus on a formal definition of an echo chamber in the literature and opt for their own, under which an echo chamber exists when the leaning of content a user receives agrees with the leaning of what they share
span.quote: As there is no consensus on a formal definition in the literature, we opt for this definition, which is general enough and reasonably captures the essence of the phenomenon

span.label: A term is borrowed from another field with its unit of analysis changed, which the authors state.
span.note: what this limits: any comparison with the gatekeeping literature: in media and communication studies gatekeepers are media sources acting as filters, whereas here they are individual users identified by their joint consumption and production leaning
span.quote: Gatekeepers are defined in media and communication studies as media sources that act as filters (or ‘gatekeepers’) of information [27]. In our case, we consider consumption and production of content jointly, and define gatekeepers as users who consume content from both sides of the political spectrum but only produce content from one side

span.label: A second definition of the same category was tested and its results not presented.
span.note: what this limits: the gatekeeper results reported here: the authors also tested a different definition - high consumption variance with low production variance - found the results almost identical, and did not present them explicitly
span.quote: We also experimented with a different definition of gatekeepers – users who have a high consumption variance and low production variance. This definition captures a slightly broader set of users (compared to Equation 5), e.g., users who consume from both ends of the political spectrum and produce balanced ‘centrist’ content. The results were almost identical to the ones reported above in Section 5.3, and so we do not present them explicitly

span.label: What the identified users are actually doing is left open by the authors.
span.note: what this limits: any interpretation of the gatekeeper class: the authors say it is not clear from their analysis what such users are doing, so the label marks a position on two measures and not a motive
span.quote: Nevertheless, from our current analysis, it is not clear if such users act as open-minded net-citizens

span.label: ten-fold cross-validation of the partisan and gatekeeper classification model
span.note: eliminates: an accuracy figure earned on the same data the classifier was fitted to
span.quote: The accuracy of the classification model is shown in Table 4 (average for 10-fold cross-validation) for partisans (p) and gatekeepers (д).

span.label: echo chamber
span.quote: We say that an echo chamber exists if the political leaning of the content that users receive from the network agrees with that of the content they share. As there is no consensus on a formal definition in the literature, we opt for this definition, which is general enough and reasonably captures the essence of the phenomenon

span.label: gatekeeper
span.quote: Gatekeepers are defined in media and communication studies as media sources that act as filters (or ‘gatekeepers’) of information [27]. In our case, we consider consumption and production of content jointly, and define gatekeepers as users who consume content from both sides of the political spectrum but only produce content from one side. These users block or filter information from one side, and hence can be considered gatekeepers

span.label: media sources
span.quote: Gatekeeping is a term commonly used in communication studies to refer to news media sources that act as filters of information

span.label: leaning
span.quote: engadget.com/2017/07/05/obama-foundation-social-media-echo-chambers 2We use “leaning” as a score that quantifies alignment with one political side. Similar terms in the literature include “ideology,” “polarity,” or “ideological stance

span.label: consumption variance
span.quote: We also experimented with a different definition of gatekeepers – users who have a high consumption variance and low production variance

span.label: price of bipartisanship
span.quote: This finding hints at the existence of a “price of bipartisanship,” required to be paid by users who try to bridge echo chambers

span.label: follow → content consumption
span.note: THE INDEXING / PROXY RELATION - Q-299. `from` STANDS IN FOR `to`. We have no type for it: `causes` asserts production, and `operationalised-as` says the authors CHOSE a measure, whereas a proxy claim says THIS STANDS IN FOR WHAT WE ACTUALLY CARE ABOUT AND WE KNOW IT IS NOT THE SAME THING. Measured at 8% of papers. A measurement substitution stated plainly: 'we use the “follow” relationship as a proxy for THE ACTUAL CONTENT CONSUMPTION'. The word `actual` is doing the same work as amodei2016's 'really care about' - the authors marking the distance between what they measured and what they meant.
span.quote: That is, we use the “follow” relationship as a proxy for the actual content consumption.

span.label: an echo chamber - AS AGREEMENT BETWEEN TWO PER-USER SCORES: it exists, for this paper, when the leaning of the content a user receives agrees with the leaning of what they share; not a group, not a network structure, not an isolation measure, but a correlation computed per user - and the authors adopt it because the literature offers no consensus formal definition to inherit
span.quote: We say that an echo chamber exists if the political leaning of the content that users receive from the network agrees with that of the content they share. As there is no consensus on a formal definition in the literature, we opt for this definition, which is general enough and reasonably captures the essence of the phenomenon

span.label: a gatekeeper - AN INDIVIDUAL USER, NOT A MEDIA SOURCE: communication studies gives the word to institutions that filter what passes into a channel, and this paper reassigns it to a person at a particular position on two scores, stating the earlier sense and supplying a bridging argument - that such users block information from one side, and hence can be considered gatekeepers
span.quote: Gatekeepers are defined in media and communication studies as media sources that act as filters (or ‘gatekeepers’) of information [27]. In our case, we consider consumption and production of content jointly, and define gatekeepers as users who consume content from both sides of the political spectrum but only produce content from one side. These users block or filter information from one side, and hence can be considered gatekeepers

span.label: leaning - A STIPULATED SCORE, WITH ITS OWN SYNONYMS NAMED IN THE FOOTNOTE THAT STIPULATES IT: the authors define it as a score quantifying alignment with one political side and list the terms the literature uses for the same thing, so four words - leaning, ideology, polarity, ideological stance - are declared interchangeable by the paper itself
span.quote: as a score that quantifies alignment with one political side. Similar terms in the literature include “ideology,” “polarity,” or “ideological stance
